claim: The Hassenstein-Reichardt (HR) elementary motion detector model has been used to analyze how the visual system detects image motion.
source: The problem has long been analysed using mathematical models that compare two adjacent viewpoints, of which the Hassenstein-Reichardt (HR) elementary motion detector (EMD; Hassenstein and Reichardt, 1956; Figure 1A) or Barlow-Levick (BL) model (Barlow and Levick, 1965; Figure 1B) are both widely canvassed.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hassenstein and Reichardt, 1956 and reference to historical use of the model.

claim: The Barlow-Levick (BL) model has been used to analyze how the visual system detects image motion.
source: The problem has long been analysed using mathematical models that compare two adjacent viewpoints, of which the Hassenstein-Reichardt (HR) elementary motion detector (EMD; Hassenstein and Reichardt, 1956; Figure 1A) or Barlow-Levick (BL) model (Barlow and Levick, 1965; Figure 1B) are both widely canvassed.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barlow and Levick, 1965 and reference to historical use of the model.

claim: Both HR and BL models compare two visual inputs separated in time and space and simulate motion detection well.
source: Both models compare two visual inputs separated in time and space and simulate motion detection well (Haag et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Haag et al., 2016.

claim: The exact neural mechanism underlying the detection of direction by motion-sensing cells is still understood only imperfectly.
source: However, the exact neural mechanism underlying the detection of direction by motion-sensing cells is still understood only imperfectly.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Visual processing in flies occurs consecutively in four retinotopically organised neuropile relays beneath the photoreceptor layer.
source: Visual processing in flies occurs consecutively in four retinotopically organised neuropile relays beneath the photoreceptor layer (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C which shows the four neuropiles.

claim: Each neuropile comprises an array of repeating modules corresponding to the hexagonal lattice of ommatidia in the overlying compound eye.
source: Each neuropile comprises an array of repeating modules corresponding to the hexagonal lattice of ommatidia in the overlying compound eye (Braitenberg, 1970; Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Takemura et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Braitenberg, 1970; Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Takemura et al., 2008.

claim: Visual signals generated by photoreceptors R1-R6 are transmitted to two matched classes of large paired interneurons, L1 and L2, and a third, L3, in the lamina.
source: Visual signals generated by photoreceptors, R1-R6, are transmitted to two matched classes of large paired interneurons, L1 and L2, and a third, L3, in the first neuropile, or lamina (Figure 1C) (Meinertzhagen and O'Neil, 1991; Rivera-Alba et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Meinertzhagen and O'Neil, 1991; Rivera-Alba et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 1C.

claim: L1 and L2 are analogous to ON and OFF bipolar cells in the vertebrate retina.
source: Like ON and OFF bipolar cells in the vertebrate retina (Wässle, 2004; Dowling, 2012), the visual pathways split at the first synapse, with L1 and L2 as the main inputs (Rister et al., 2007), to separate ON- and OFF-edge motion pathways, respectively (Joesch et al., 2010; Clark et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wässle, 2004; Dowling, 2012; Rister et al., 2007; Joesch et al., 2010; Clark et al., 2011.

claim: The visual pathways split at the first synapse, with L1 and L2 as the main inputs to separate ON- and OFF-edge motion pathways, respectively.
source: Like ON and OFF bipolar cells in the vertebrate retina (Wässle, 2004; Dowling, 2012), the visual pathways split at the first synapse, with L1 and L2 as the main inputs (Rister et al., 2007), to separate ON- and OFF-edge motion pathways, respectively (Joesch et al., 2010; Clark et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rister et al., 2007; Joesch et al., 2010; Clark et al., 2011.

claim: ON-edge signals are locally computed on the dendritic arbours of columnar cells, T4, in the most proximal stratum M10 of the medulla.
source: ON-edge signals are then locally computed on the dendritic arbours of columnar cells, T4, in the most proximal stratum M10 of the second neuropile, or medulla (Fisher et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fisher et al., 2015.

claim: T4 cells respond to visual motion in a directionally-selective manner.
source: These cells respond to visual motion in a directionally-selective manner (Maisak et al., 2013), and have four subtypes, T4a-T4d (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maisak et al., 2013.

claim: T4 cells have four subtypes, T4a-T4d.
source: These cells respond to visual motion in a directionally-selective manner (Maisak et al., 2013), and have four subtypes, T4a-T4d (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Takemura et al., 2013.

claim: Each T4 subtype is tuned to one of four cardinal directions of stimulus motion: front-to-back (T4a), back-to-front (T4b), upward (T4c) and downward (T4d).
source: Each subtype is tuned to one of four cardinal directions of stimulus motion, front-to-back (T4a), back-to-front (T4b), upward (T4c) and downward (T4d) (Maisak et al., 2013), approximately one each per unit column of the medulla (Takemura et al., 2013; Mauss et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maisak et al., 2013; Takemura et al., 2013; Mauss et al., 2014.

claim: There is approximately one T4 cell of each subtype per unit column of the medulla.
source: Each subtype is tuned to one of four cardinal directions of stimulus motion, front-to-back (T4a), back-to-front (T4b), upward (T4c) and downward (T4d) (Maisak et al., 2013), approximately one each per unit column of the medulla (Takemura et al., 2013; Mauss et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Takemura et al., 2013; Mauss et al., 2014.

claim: Each T4 subtype projects its terminal to a specific stratum, one of four in the lobula plate.
source: Each in turn projects its terminal to a specific stratum, one of four in the motion-sensing fourth neuropile, the lobula plate (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C.

claim: T4 signals from hundreds of columns sum to generate wide-field motion responses in target, directionally-selective tangential cells.
source: There, T4 signals from hundreds of columns sum to generate wide-field motion responses in target, directionally-selective tangential cells (Borst et al., 2010), aided by various lobula plate interneurons (Mauss et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Borst et al., 2010; Mauss et al., 2015.

claim: A previous connectomic study using serial-section EM identified Mi1 and Tm3 as the direct pathways between L1 and T4.
source: A recent connectomic study using serial-section EM (ssEM) identified two medulla cell types, Mi1 and Tm3, as the direct pathways between L1 and T4 (Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Takemura et al., 2013.

claim: The weighted centre of the Mi1-mediated receptive field is displaced from that of the Tm3-mediated subfield.
source: Detailed analyses revealed that the weighted centre of the Mi1-mediated receptive field is displaced from that of the Tm3-mediated subfield, and that the direction of displacement between the two subfields aligns in ~70% of cases with T4's preferred direction (Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Takemura et al., 2013.

claim: The direction of displacement between Mi1 and Tm3 subfields aligns in ~70% of cases with T4's preferred direction.
source: Detailed analyses revealed that the weighted centre of the Mi1-mediated receptive field is displaced from that of the Tm3-mediated subfield, and that the direction of displacement between the two subfields aligns in ~70% of cases with T4's preferred direction (Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Takemura et al., 2013.

claim: Mi1 exhibits a peak light response later than that in Tm3.
source: Electrophysiological recordings demonstrate a temporal offset between the responses of the two cell types: Mi1 exhibits a peak light response later than that in Tm3 (Behnia et al., 2014), although the time difference (~15 ms) is probably too small to account for T4's measured temporal frequency optimum of ~1 Hz (Maisak et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Behnia et al., 2014.

claim: The time difference between Mi1 and Tm3 responses (~15 ms) is probably too small to account for T4's measured temporal frequency optimum of ~1 Hz.
source: Electrophysiological recordings demonstrate a temporal offset between the responses of the two cell types: Mi1 exhibits a peak light response later than that in Tm3 (Behnia et al., 2014), although the time difference (~15 ms) is probably too small to account for T4's measured temporal frequency optimum of ~1 Hz (Maisak et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cited data in Behnia et al., 2014 and Maisak et al., 2013.

claim: The direction of spatial offsets from Tm3 to Mi1 generally matches the requirements of non-delay and delay input channels of a BL-type detector.
source: The direction of spatial offsets from Tm3 to Mi1, generally consistent with T4's preferred direction, matches the requirements of non-delay and delay input channels of a BL-type detector.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial offset data and the requirements of the BL model.

claim: A BL-type detector requires Mi1 and Tm3 inputs to T4 to have different signs.
source: First, a BL-type detector requires Mi1 and Tm3 inputs to T4 to have different signs (Figure 1B); this is not supported by available neurotransmitter information (see below).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the BL model requirements and inference from neurotransmitter data.

claim: Mi1 and Tm3 synapses on T4 dendrites are distributed with substantial overlap.
source: Second, whereas each T4 dendrite is orientated primarily in a direction aligned with its directional preference (Takemura et al., 2013), Mi1 and Tm3 synapses on those dendrites are distributed with substantial overlap.
evidence: This is a statement about the observed distribution of synapses, with reference to Takemura et al., 2013 for dendrite orientation.

claim: Each T4 dendrite is orientated primarily in a direction aligned with its directional preference.
source: Second, whereas each T4 dendrite is orientated primarily in a direction aligned with its directional preference (Takemura et al., 2013), Mi1 and Tm3 synapses on those dendrites are distributed with substantial overlap.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Takemura et al., 2013.

claim: Mi1 has a general role in ON-motion detection.
source: Third, although recent experiments confirm a general role for Mi1 in ON-motion detection, they suggest that Tm3 is required for responses only to fast-motion stimuli (Ammer et al., 2015), so that other inputs must be active under slow-motion stimulus conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ammer et al., 2015.

claim: Tm3 is required for responses only to fast-motion stimuli.
source: Third, although recent experiments confirm a general role for Mi1 in ON-motion detection, they suggest that Tm3 is required for responses only to fast-motion stimuli (Ammer et al., 2015), so that other inputs must be active under slow-motion stimulus conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ammer et al., 2015.

claim: Other inputs to T4 must be active under slow-motion stimulus conditions.
source: Third, although recent experiments confirm a general role for Mi1 in ON-motion detection, they suggest that Tm3 is required for responses only to fast-motion stimuli (Ammer et al., 2015), so that other inputs must be active under slow-motion stimulus conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that Tm3 is only required for fast motion (Ammer et al., 2015).

claim: The study used focussed ion-beam milling scanning electron microscopy (FIBSEM) to reconstruct T4 cells and their presynaptic partners.
source: Here, we use a superior EM technique to reconstruct T4 cells and their presynaptic partners, and provide a comprehensive anatomical view of this critical step in fly motion vision.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and detailed in the Methods section.

claim: The study imaged a ~40 × 40 x 80 µm volume at an isotropic resolution of 10 nm per voxel.
source: Briefly, we imaged a ~40 × 40 x 80 µm volume at an isotropic resolution of 10 nm per voxel, annotated ~53,500 presynaptic sites and ~315,500 postsynaptic sites, and reconstructed >900 neuron bodies including >60 T4 cells.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collection.

claim: The study annotated ~53,500 presynaptic sites and ~315,500 postsynaptic sites.
source: Briefly, we imaged a ~40 × 40 x 80 µm volume at an isotropic resolution of 10 nm per voxel, annotated ~53,500 presynaptic sites and ~315,500 postsynaptic sites, and reconstructed >900 neuron bodies including >60 T4 cells.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data annotation.

claim: The study reconstructed >900 neuron bodies including >60 T4 cells.
source: Briefly, we imaged a ~40 × 40 x 80 µm volume at an isotropic resolution of 10 nm per voxel, annotated ~53,500 presynaptic sites and ~315,500 postsynaptic sites, and reconstructed >900 neuron bodies including >60 T4 cells.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental reconstruction results.

claim: The dataset volume comprised seven medulla columns: a central 'Home' column and its six immediate neighbours.
source: The dataset volume comprised seven medulla columns: a central 'Home' column and its six immediate neighbours (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a description of the dataset structure, supported by Figure 1D.

claim: Mi1-Home contacted >20 T4 cells, forming 2–43 synapses onto each.
source: We found Mi1-Home contacted >20 T4 cells, forming 2–43 synapses onto each.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the connectome reconstruction.

claim: Only four T4s received >35 contacts from Mi1-Home.
source: Among these, only four T4s received >35 such contacts.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the connectome reconstruction.

claim: The four T4s that received >35 contacts from Mi1-Home included one of each subtype, T4a-T4d.
source: They included one of each subtype, T4a-T4d, as identified by the distinctive orientation of their dendrites (Takemura et al., 2013) (Figures 2A and 4C–4E).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figures 2A and 4C-4E and citation to Takemura et al., 2013.

claim: Eight medulla neuron types account for inputs to the T4 dendrites.
source: Reconstructed cell shapes revealed eight medulla neuron types that account for inputs to the T4 dendrites (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 2A.

claim: The study confirmed previously reported inputs from neurons Mi1, Tm3, C3, Mi4, Mi9 and T4 itself.
source: We confirmed previously reported inputs from neurons Mi1, Tm3, C3, Mi4, Mi9 and T4 itself (Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a confirmation of previous findings, with citation to Takemura et al., 2013.

claim: The study identified a previously undescribed TmY neuron, called TmY15.
source: Comparing the remaining reconstructed cells with light microscopy data further identified a previously undescribed TmY neuron, which we call TmY15 (Figure 2A and B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and neurites of a new large tangential cell, which we call CT1 (Figure 2A and C–E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a new finding from the study, supported by Figures 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The study identified neurites of a new large tangential cell, called CT1.
source: Comparing the remaining reconstructed cells with light microscopy data further identified a previously undescribed TmY neuron, which we call TmY15 (Figure 2A and B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and neurites of a new large tangential cell, which we call CT1 (Figure 2A and C–E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a new finding from the study, supported by Figures 2A, 2C-E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CT1 spans the opposing faces of medulla stratum M10 and lobula stratum Lo1 as a single giant neuron.
source: CT1 spans the opposing faces of medulla stratum M10 and lobula stratum Lo1 that contains dendrites of T4's counterpart, T5, as a single giant neuron (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a description of CT1 anatomy, supported by Figure 2C.

claim: CT1 terminal arbours show a strikingly regular pattern in each medulla and lobula column.
source: Its terminal arbours show a strikingly regular pattern in each medulla and lobula column (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which is also confirmed by EM reconstructions (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a description of CT1 anatomy, supported by Figures 2D, 2E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In each column, CT1 receives a few synaptic inputs from Mi1, Mi9 and all T4 subtypes.
source: In each column, CT1 receives a few synaptic inputs from Mi1, Mi9 and all T4 subtypes (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 2F.

claim: Each T4 receives >200 synaptic inputs in total.
source: We next examined the number of T4 inputs from each of these cell types (Figure 3). Each T4 receives >200 synaptic inputs in total, and Mi1 and Tm3 cells are indeed the largest contributors with 35.0% and 16.1% of the total, respectively (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 3.

claim: Mi1 and Tm3 cells are the largest contributors to T4 inputs with 35.0% and 16.1% of the total, respectively.
source: We next examined the number of T4 inputs from each of these cell types (Figure 3). Each T4 receives >200 synaptic inputs in total, and Mi1 and Tm3 cells are indeed the largest contributors with 35.0% and 16.1% of the total, respectively (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 3.

claim: Total synaptic inputs from Mi1 and Tm3 to the four T4 subtypes in the FIBSEM reconstruction totalled 33% more than in the previous ssEM connectome.
source: Endorsing improved completeness of the new FIBSEM reconstruction, total synaptic inputs from Mi1 and Tm3 to the four T4 subtypes (116, 109, 113, and 104, respectively), totalled 33% more than in the previous ssEM connectome (97, 69, 85 and 81) (Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of quantitative results between the current and previous study, with citation to Takemura et al., 2013.

claim: Mi9 provides 13.3% of T4 inputs.
source: However, we identified more than previously reported, primarily because many of these synapses are located in the periphery of a T4's dendrites and were therefore excluded from an earlier account (Takemura et al., 2013), which sampled densely only a single column. Secondarily, we benefit from greater image quality of FIBSEM. Their wider contribution is nevertheless significant: 13.3% (Mi9), 6.4% (Mi4) and 3.9% (C3), in aggregate ~24% of the total (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 3.

claim: Mi4 provides 6.4% of T4 inputs.
source: However, we identified more than previously reported, primarily because many of these synapses are located in the periphery of a T4's dendrites and were therefore excluded from an earlier account (Takemura et al., 2013), which sampled densely only a single column. Secondarily, we benefit from greater image quality of FIBSEM. Their wider contribution is nevertheless significant: 13.3% (Mi9), 6.4% (Mi4) and 3.9% (C3), in aggregate ~24% of the total (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 3.

claim: C3 provides 3.9% of T4 inputs.
source: However, we identified more than previously reported, primarily because many of these synapses are located in the periphery of a T4's dendrites and were therefore excluded from an earlier account (Takemura et al., 2013), which sampled densely only a single column. Secondarily, we benefit from greater image quality of FIBSEM. Their wider contribution is nevertheless significant: 13.3% (Mi9), 6.4% (Mi4) and 3.9% (C3), in aggregate ~24% of the total (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 3.

claim: Mi4, Mi9, and C3 together account for ~24% of T4 inputs.
source: However, we identified more than previously reported, primarily because many of these synapses are located in the periphery of a T4's dendrites and were therefore excluded from an earlier account (Takemura et al., 2013), which sampled densely only a single column. Secondarily, we benefit from greater image quality of FIBSEM. Their wider contribution is nevertheless significant: 13.3% (Mi9), 6.4% (Mi4) and 3.9% (C3), in aggregate ~24% of the total (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 3.

claim: The new FIBSEM reconstruction identified many more connections than the previous ssEM study which found 4 Mi4 inputs, 6 Mi9 inputs, and 5 C3 inputs.
source: The new FIBSEM reconstruction identified many more connections than the previous ssEM study which found 4 Mi4 inputs, 6 Mi9 inputs, and 5 C3 inputs (Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of quantitative results between the current and previous study, with citation to Takemura et al., 2013.

claim: TmY15 and CT1 together account for ~15% of T4 inputs.
source: The newly identified TmY15 and CT1 cells together account for another ~15% of T4 inputs (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 3.

claim: A T4 cell connects reciprocally to other T4s in neighbouring columns.
source: In addition, a T4 cell also connects reciprocally to other T4s in neighbouring columns.
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction.

claim: An Mi10 neuron makes a few input synapses (~0.6%) onto T4s.
source: Only very few synapses onto T4s were from other cell types or could not be identified: an Mi10 neuron makes a few input synapses (~0.6%), with the remaining 3.1% from several unidentified profiles that left the reconstructed volume, each contacting a T4 at ≤3 synapses (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 3B.

claim: 3.1% of T4 inputs are from several unidentified profiles that left the reconstructed volume, each contacting a T4 at ≤3 synapses.
source: Only very few synapses onto T4s were from other cell types or could not be identified: an Mi10 neuron makes a few input synapses (~0.6%), with the remaining 3.1% from several unidentified profiles that left the reconstructed volume, each contacting a T4 at ≤3 synapses (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 3B.

claim: At least some of the unidentified synapses onto T4 are likely to be from branches of other T4s that reside outside the imaged region.
source: At least some of these unidentified synapses are likely to be from branches of other T4s that reside outside the imaged region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the connectome data.

claim: The dense FIBSEM reconstruction captures all input cell types to T4.
source: We therefore reason that our dense FIBSEM reconstruction captures all input cell types to T4 and is now reliably definitive.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comprehensiveness of the reconstruction.

claim: Each T4 subtype receives input from multiple Mi1s, with the strongest from the Home Mi1 and weaker inputs from surrounding Mi1s.
source: Each T4 subtype receives input from multiple Mi1s, with the strongest from the Home Mi1 and weaker inputs from surrounding Mi1s (Figure 4A); these spread along the shafts of the T4 dendrites (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figures 4A and 4C.

claim: Mi1 synapses spread along the shafts of the T4 dendrites.
source: Each T4 subtype receives input from multiple Mi1s, with the strongest from the Home Mi1 and weaker inputs from surrounding Mi1s (Figure 4A); these spread along the shafts of the T4 dendrites (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: Tm3 synapses appear to distribute evenly over the T4 dendrites.
source: Likewise, Tm3 synapses appear to distribute evenly over the T4 dendrites (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 4D.

claim: Mi1 cells can be readily assigned to specific columns.
source: However, while Mi1 cells can be readily assigned to specific columns, Tm3s occupy more variable positions in the column periphery, and cannot be so assigned (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tm3s occupy more variable positions in the column periphery, and cannot be assigned to specific columns.
source: However, while Mi1 cells can be readily assigned to specific columns, Tm3s occupy more variable positions in the column periphery, and cannot be so assigned (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Wide collaterals of Tm3 cells in strata M1 and M5 extend beyond the 7-column region.
source: Calculating anatomical receptive fields (Takemura et al., 2013), is also limited because wide collaterals of Tm3 cells in strata M1 and M5 (Figure 2A) extend beyond the 7-column region.
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 2A.

claim: The reconstructed Tm3s receive some input from columns not contained in the FIBSEM image stack.
source: The reconstructed Tm3s therefore receive some input from columns not contained in the FIBSEM image stack used here and which we therefore could not trace.
evidence: This is an inference based on the extent of Tm3 arbors.

claim: The accuracy with which potential spatial offsets between Tm3 and other cell types could be determined is limited.
source: This limits the accuracy with which potential spatial offsets between Tm3 and other cell types could be determined (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and Discussion).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the data, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Inputs to T4 from Mi4 and Mi9 are noticeably segregated from each other.
source: Inputs to T4 from Mi4 and Mi9 are noticeably segregated from each other (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figures 4A and 4C.

claim: Mi9's input synapses always cluster at the tips of the T4 dendrites.
source: Significantly, Mi9's input synapses always cluster at the tips of the T4 dendrites while Mi4's inputs localize to their bases (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: Mi4's inputs localize to the bases of T4 dendrites.
source: Significantly, Mi9's input synapses always cluster at the tips of the T4 dendrites while Mi4's inputs localize to their bases (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: Inputs from other T4 cells clustered towards T4's dendrite tips.
source: Inputs from other T4 cells also clustered towards T4's dendrite tips (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 4E.

claim: T4-T4 synapses showed striking subtype selectivity connecting with cells with the same direction preference.
source: The T4-T4 synapses showed striking subtype selectivity connecting with cells with the same direction preference, apparently qualifying a group of T4s to signal each other about a particular stimulus direction.
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction.

claim: T4-T4 subtype selectivity was observed without exception in every T4-T4 contact.
source: This subtype selectivity was observed without exception in every T4-T4 contact.
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction.

claim: The retinotopic positions of the presynaptic T4s lie relative to the postsynaptic T4 in a direction opposite to the cell's preferred direction.
source: The retinotopic positions of the presynaptic T4s lie relative to the postsynaptic T4 in a direction opposite to the cell's preferred direction (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 4E.

claim: C3 and CT1 made synapses at the bases of T4 dendrites.
source: Like Mi4, C3 and CT1 also made synapses at the bases (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: CT1 connections are displaced from the Mi1 centre in a manner very similar to that of Mi4 and C3.
source: Even though CT1 is a wide-field neuron (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), its connections are displaced from the Mi1 centre in a manner very similar to that of Mi4 and C3 (Figure 4B), suggesting that each columnar arbour may serve a local computational role.
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figures 2C, 4B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each columnar arbour of CT1 may serve a local computational role.
source: Even though CT1 is a wide-field neuron (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), its connections are displaced from the Mi1 centre in a manner very similar to that of Mi4 and C3 (Figure 4B), suggesting that each columnar arbour may serve a local computational role.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial distribution of CT1 connections.

claim: TmY15 is presynaptic to T4s with a branching arbour extending more widely than the 7-column area in stratum M10.
source: Finally, TmY15 is presynaptic to T4s with a branching arbour extending more widely than the 7-column area in stratum M10 (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three TmY15 cells were reconstructed in the 7-column volume, of which two are only partial.
source: We have reconstructed three TmY15 cells in the 7-column volume, of which two are only partial, suggesting that this cell type is distributed less frequently than one cell per column.
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction.

claim: TmY15 is distributed less frequently than one cell per column.
source: We have reconstructed three TmY15 cells in the 7-column volume, of which two are only partial, suggesting that this cell type is distributed less frequently than one cell per column.
evidence: This is an inference based on the number of reconstructed TmY15 cells.

claim: TmY15 synaptic inputs were rather uniformly distributed over T4's dendrites.
source: Its synaptic inputs were rather uniformly distributed over T4's dendrites (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 4D.

claim: Immunolabelling studies have suggested that C3 is GABAergic.
source: Immunolabelling studies have suggested that C3 is GABAergic (Kolodziejczyk et al., 2008) while Mi1 expresses choline acetyltransferase (Hasegawa et al., 2011; Pankova and Borst, 2017), suggesting it is cholinergic.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kolodziejczyk et al., 2008.

claim: Mi1 expresses choline acetyltransferase, suggesting it is cholinergic.
source: Immunolabelling studies have suggested that C3 is GABAergic (Kolodziejczyk et al., 2008) while Mi1 expresses choline acetyltransferase (Hasegawa et al., 2011; Pankova and Borst, 2017), suggesting it is cholinergic.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hasegawa et al., 2011; Pankova and Borst, 2017.

claim: Immunolabeling results using anti-GAD1, anti-ChAT and anti-VGlut confirm that C3 uses GABA and Mi1 uses acetylcholine.
source: Our immunolabeling results using anti-GAD1, anti-ChAT and anti-VGlut confirm these results for C3 and Mi1 and further suggest that GABA, acetylcholine and glutamate are the respective transmitters for Mi4, Tm3 and Mi9 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from immunolabeling experiments, supported by Figure 5.

claim: GABA, acetylcholine and glutamate are the respective transmitters for Mi4, Tm3 and Mi9.
source: Our immunolabeling results using anti-GAD1, anti-ChAT and anti-VGlut confirm these results for C3 and Mi1 and further suggest that GABA, acetylcholine and glutamate are the respective transmitters for Mi4, Tm3 and Mi9 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from immunolabeling experiments, supported by Figure 5.

claim: Cell-type-specific transcript profiling studies support the neurotransmitter identities for Mi4, Tm3, and Mi9.
source: These results are also supported by cell-type-specific transcript profiling studies (L Henry, F Davis and S Eddy, personal communication).
evidence: The claim is supported by a personal communication citation.

claim: Anti-GAD1 immunolabelling reveals that CT1 and TmY15 appear to use GABA.
source: In addition, anti-GAD1 immunolabelling reveals that CT1 and TmY15 appear to use GABA (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from immunolabeling experiments, supported by Figure 5.

claim: T4 dendrites receive both excitatory and inhibitory inputs.
source: These considerations indicate that T4 dendrites receive both excitatory and inhibitory inputs and, together with the EM data, allowed us to examine the distribution of inputs of different predicted signs: the synapses from C3/Mi4/CT1 onto the T4 dendrite base all appear to be GABA-ergic and therefore inhibitory, whereas those from Mi1 and Tm3 along the shaft of the T4 dendrite are putatively cholinergic, and therefore most likely to be excitatory (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference based on neurotransmitter identity and EM data, supported by Figure 6B.

claim: Synapses from C3/Mi4/CT1 onto the T4 dendrite base all appear to be GABA-ergic and therefore inhibitory.
source: These considerations indicate that T4 dendrites receive both excitatory and inhibitory inputs and, together with the EM data, allowed us to examine the distribution of inputs of different predicted signs: the synapses from C3/Mi4/CT1 onto the T4 dendrite base all appear to be GABA-ergic and therefore inhibitory, whereas those from Mi1 and Tm3 along the shaft of the T4 dendrite are putatively cholinergic, and therefore most likely to be excitatory (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference based on neurotransmitter identity and EM data, supported by Figure 6B.

claim: Synapses from Mi1 and Tm3 along the shaft of the T4 dendrite are putatively cholinergic, and therefore most likely to be excitatory.
source: These considerations indicate that T4 dendrites receive both excitatory and inhibitory inputs and, together with the EM data, allowed us to examine the distribution of inputs of different predicted signs: the synapses from C3/Mi4/CT1 onto the T4 dendrite base all appear to be GABA-ergic and therefore inhibitory, whereas those from Mi1 and Tm3 along the shaft of the T4 dendrite are putatively cholinergic, and therefore most likely to be excitatory (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference based on neurotransmitter identity and EM data, supported by Figure 6B.

claim: Mi9's input at the T4 dendrite tip, putatively glutamatergic, may be either excitatory or inhibitory, depending on receptor expression at this synapse.
source: Mi9's input at the T4 dendrite tip, putatively glutamatergic, may be either excitatory or inhibitory, depending on receptor expression at this synapse, given that glutamatergic neurotransmission can be inhibitory in Drosophila (Liu and Wilson, 2013; Mauss et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on neurotransmitter identity and knowledge from citations to Liu and Wilson, 2013; Mauss et al., 2015.

claim: Glutamatergic neurotransmission can be inhibitory in Drosophila.
source: Mi9's input at the T4 dendrite tip, putatively glutamatergic, may be either excitatory or inhibitory, depending on receptor expression at this synapse, given that glutamatergic neurotransmission can be inhibitory in Drosophila (Liu and Wilson, 2013; Mauss et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu and Wilson, 2013; Mauss et al., 2015.

claim: T4-T4 synapses are primarily cholinergic, and thus most likely to be excitatory.
source: T4-T4 synapses, also at the dendritic tips, are primarily cholinergic (Mauss et al., 2014; Shinomiya et al., 2014), and thus most likely to be excitatory.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mauss et al., 2014; Shinomiya et al., 2014.

claim: Inputs from Mi4, C3 and CT1 onto T4's dendrite bases could form one input channel of a BL motion detector.
source: Of the synaptic inputs to T4 that are anatomically qualified to serve as two channels of a motion detector, several could support BL motion detectors (Figure 1B). First, inputs from Mi4, C3 and CT1 onto T4's dendrite bases, which could form one input channel, are putatively inhibitory and therefore opposite in sign to excitatory input from Mi1 and Tm3 which could form another channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical and neurotransmitter data.

claim: Inputs from Mi1 and Tm3 could form another channel of a BL motion detector.
source: Of the synaptic inputs to T4 that are anatomically qualified to serve as two channels of a motion detector, several could support BL motion detectors (Figure 1B). First, inputs from Mi4, C3 and CT1 onto T4's dendrite bases, which could form one input channel, are putatively inhibitory and therefore opposite in sign to excitatory input from Mi1 and Tm3 which could form another channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical and neurotransmitter data.

claim: The vectors of physiological direction preference of each T4 match those measured in a direction from excitatory inputs (dendrite shaft, Mi1/Tm3) to inhibitory inputs (dendrite base, Mi4/C3/CT1) in accordance with a BL motion detector.
source: Second, the vectors of physiological direction preference of each T4, as inferred from dendrite orientation, match those measured in a direction from excitatory inputs (dendrite shaft, Mi1/Tm3) to inhibitory inputs (dendrite base, Mi4/C3/CT1) in accordance with a BL motion detector (Figure 6B; cf. Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical and neurotransmitter data, supported by Figures 6B and 1B.

claim: The inhibitory inputs to T4 arrive via a di- or trisynaptic pathway from L1, via L5 or Mi1 and others (e.g. L1→L5→Mi4→T4).
source: Third, the inhibitory inputs arrive via a di- or trisynaptic pathway from L1, via L5 or Mi1 and others (e.g. L1→L5→Mi4→T4) (Figure 6A; see also Figure 3a in ref 16).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 6A.

claim: Putatively excitatory inputs from Mi1 and Tm3 onto T4's dendrite shafts are monosynaptic.
source: By contrast, putatively excitatory inputs from Mi1 and Tm3 onto T4's dendrite shafts are monosynaptic (Figure 6) suggesting a possible time delay between excitatory and inhibitory channels, but one that would be too short alone to account for the temporal frequency optimum in T4 cells of about 1 Hz (Maisak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a result from the connectome reconstruction, supported by Figure 6.

claim: There is a possible time delay between excitatory and inhibitory channels to T4, but one that would be too short alone to account for the temporal frequency optimum in T4 cells of about 1 Hz.
source: By contrast, putatively excitatory inputs from Mi1 and Tm3 onto T4's dendrite shafts are monosynaptic (Figure 6) suggesting a possible time delay between excitatory and inhibitory channels, but one that would be too short alone to account for the temporal frequency optimum in T4 cells of about 1 Hz (Maisak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the connectome data and citation to Maisak et al., 2013.

claim: A role for Mi1 and Tm3 in T4's motion computation has been confirmed.
source: Among the potential inputs that could serve as HR motion detectors we first consider Mi1 and Tm3, as previously suggested (Takemura et al., 2013). A role for these cells in T4's motion computation has been confirmed: Mi1 block flies are motion blind to ON-edge stimuli, while Tm3 input is specifically required to detect fast ON-edge motion in the preferred direction (Ammer et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Takemura et al., 2013 and Ammer et al., 2015.

claim: Mi1 block flies are motion blind to ON-edge stimuli.
source: Among the potential inputs that could serve as HR motion detectors we first consider Mi1 and Tm3, as previously suggested (Takemura et al., 2013). A role for these cells in T4's motion computation has been confirmed: Mi1 block flies are motion blind to ON-edge stimuli, while Tm3 input is specifically required to detect fast ON-edge motion in the preferred direction (Ammer et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ammer et al., 2015.

claim: The polarities of transmission at both Mi1 and Tm3 inputs are likely to be the same because both appear to use acetylcholine as a neurotransmitter.
source: The polarities of transmission at both Mi1 and Tm3 inputs are likely to be the same because both appear to use acetylcholine as a neurotransmitter.
evidence: This is an inference based on neurotransmitter identity.

claim: A recent calcium imaging study has shown an enhanced T4 response when both Mi1 and Tm3 are activated.
source: In fact, a recent calcium imaging study has shown an enhanced T4 response when both cells are activated (Strother et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Strother et al., 2017.

claim: Mi1 and Tm3 could function as two excitatory input channels in an HR EMD circuit.
source: Thus Mi1 and Tm3 could function as two excitatory input channels in an HR EMD circuit (Figure 1A), potentially depending on visual stimulus conditions such as different visual contrasts or velocities (Ammer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the neurotransmitter and functional data, with citation to Ammer et al., 2015.

claim: The relative timing of Mi1 and Tm3 inputs recorded by Behnia et al. (2014) is contrary to that in an HR EMD, assuming the measured directions of receptive field offsets between Mi1 and Tm3.
source: This interpretation, however, runs counter to two features. First, assuming the measured directions of receptive field offsets between Mi1 and Tm3 (Takemura et al., 2013), the relative timing of the two inputs recorded by Behnia et al. (2014) is contrary to that in an HR EMD.
evidence: This is an inference based on data from Takemura et al., 2013 and Behnia et al., 2014.

claim: The magnitude of the spatial offset between Mi1 and Tm3 appears to be very small.
source: Moreover, the magnitude of the spatial offset itself appears to be very small (Takemura et al., 2013; Borst and Helmstaedter, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Takemura et al., 2013; Borst and Helmstaedter, 2015.

claim: Uncertainties in the direction of the small anatomical offsets between Mi1 and Tm3 make it difficult to uphold the previous conclusion that these offsets provide the core of an EMD.
source: While our new data do not deny a role for Mi1 and Tm3 cells in motion detection, uncertainties in the direction of their small anatomical offsets (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2) do make it difficult to uphold our previous conclusion that these offsets provide the core of an EMD.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current data, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mi9 and T4-T4 connections that make synapses onto the leading edges of T4's dendrites could function as excitatory input channels of an HR model.
source: Two additional input cell types, Mi9 and T4-T4 connections, that make synapses onto the leading edges of T4's dendrites (Figure 4C and E) could also function as excitatory input channels of an HR model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical data, supported by Figures 4C and 4E.

claim: Mi9 and T4-T4 connections would work together with Mi1 and/or Tm3, qualified by their substantial spatial offsets.
source: In this case they would work together with Mi1 and/or Tm3, qualified by their substantial spatial offsets (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical data, supported by Figure 4B.

claim: Possible roles of Mi9 depend on the sign of the glutamatergic synapses and the nature of its light response.
source: However, possible roles of Mi9 depend on two properties of this cell type: the sign of the glutamatergic synapses and the nature of its light response – Mi9 might respond to OFF rather than ON-stimuli, with main synaptic input from L3 and Mi4 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the connectome data, supported by Figure 6A.

claim: Mi9 might respond to OFF rather than ON-stimuli, with main synaptic input from L3 and Mi4.
source: However, possible roles of Mi9 depend on two properties of this cell type: the sign of the glutamatergic synapses and the nature of its light response – Mi9 might respond to OFF rather than ON-stimuli, with main synaptic input from L3 and Mi4 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the connectome data, supported by Figure 6A.

claim: Recent imaging results indicate that Mi9 does respond to OFF stimuli and is likely to provide inhibitory input to T4 dendrites.
source: Indeed recent imaging results indicate that Mi9 does respond to OFF stimuli and is likely to provide inhibitory input to T4 dendrites (Strother et al., 2017; Arenz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Strother et al., 2017; Arenz et al., 2017.

claim: T4-T4 synapses are qualified to contribute to an HR mechanism because input from other T4s is spatially offset against the cells' preferred direction and predicted to be delayed since an additional synapse is involved.
source: T4-T4 synapses are also qualified to contribute to an HR mechanism: input from other T4s is spatially offset against the cells' preferred direction (Figure 4E) and predicted to be delayed since an additional synapse is involved (e.g. Mi1→T4→T4 vs Mi1→T4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical data, supported by Figure 4E.

claim: Blocking T4's synaptic outputs does not abolish directionally selective responses in T4.
source: However, blocking T4's synaptic outputs does not abolish directionally selective responses in T4 (Haag et al., 2016), suggesting that a mechanism based on T4-T4 synapses would, at least under some conditions, have to act in parallel with others.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Haag et al., 2016.

claim: A mechanism based on T4-T4 synapses would, at least under some conditions, have to act in parallel with others.
source: However, blocking T4's synaptic outputs does not abolish directionally selective responses in T4 (Haag et al., 2016), suggesting that a mechanism based on T4-T4 synapses would, at least under some conditions, have to act in parallel with others.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding from Haag et al., 2016.

claim: Parallel contributions of several T4 input pathways could serve to broaden the T4 response curve for stimulus velocity or the range of stimulus modalities.
source: Such parallel contributions of several T4 input pathways could, for example, serve to broaden the T4 response curve for: stimulus velocity, which peaks at a temporal frequency of ~1 Hz (Maisak et al., 2013); or the range of stimulus modalities, for example to different light intensities or stimuli of differing spectral composition.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of parallel pathways, with citation to Maisak et al., 2013.

claim: The study reports the complete set of input cell types to direction-selective T4 cells.
source: In summary, we report the complete set of input cell types to direction-selective T4 cells, and reveal that these circuits are anatomically qualified to implement direction selectivity using both HR model preferred-direction enhancement and BL model null-direction suppression, as has indeed recently been reported from imaging studies in both T4 (Haag et al., 2016) and T5 cells (Leong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: T4 circuits are anatomically qualified to implement direction selectivity using both HR model preferred-direction enhancement and BL model null-direction suppression.
source: In summary, we report the complete set of input cell types to direction-selective T4 cells, and reveal that these circuits are anatomically qualified to implement direction selectivity using both HR model preferred-direction enhancement and BL model null-direction suppression, as has indeed recently been reported from imaging studies in both T4 (Haag et al., 2016) and T5 cells (Leong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the anatomical data and supported by citations to Haag et al., 2016 and Leong et al., 2016.

claim: Imaging studies have reported that T4 cells use both HR model preferred-direction enhancement and BL model null-direction suppression.
source: In summary, we report the complete set of input cell types to direction-selective T4 cells, and reveal that these circuits are anatomically qualified to implement direction selectivity using both HR model preferred-direction enhancement and BL model null-direction suppression, as has indeed recently been reported from imaging studies in both T4 (Haag et al., 2016) and T5 cells (Leong et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Haag et al., 2016.

claim: Imaging studies have reported that T5 cells use both HR model preferred-direction enhancement and BL model null-direction suppression.
source: In summary, we report the complete set of input cell types to direction-selective T4 cells, and reveal that these circuits are anatomically qualified to implement direction selectivity using both HR model preferred-direction enhancement and BL model null-direction suppression, as has indeed recently been reported from imaging studies in both T4 (Haag et al., 2016) and T5 cells (Leong et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Leong et al., 2016.

claim: Synaptic inhibition from specific medulla cells could be required for reasons other than directional selectivity, and could function to signal something entirely different.
source: While not precluding the contribution of specific inputs to directional selectivity, synaptic inhibition from specific medulla cells could also be required for other reasons, and could function to signal something entirely different.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative functional roles of inhibitory inputs.

claim: CT1 is anatomically qualified to modulate the gain of T4 and T5 neurons in response to overall levels of motion.
source: For example, in addition to acting locally, CT1 is anatomically qualified to modulate the gain of T4 and T5 neurons in response to overall levels of motion.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of CT1 based on its anatomy.

claim: The EM findings will be essential to understanding the detection of motion, in combination with specific functional tests.
source: Whatever mechanism(s) they support, our EM findings will be essential to understanding the detection of motion, in combination with specific functional tests.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the study's findings.

claim: The heads of wild-type Canton-S female flies between 5 and 6 days post-eclosion were used for EM imaging.
source: The heads of wild-type Canton-S female flies between 5 and 6 days post-eclosion were fixed and processed for EM by high-pressure freezing/freeze substitution, according to previously reported methods (Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The brain tissue was embedded in Durcupan epoxy resin after fixation.
source: The brain tissue was embedded in Durcupan epoxy resin (Fluka) after fixation.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: A block face series of 32,000 images was acquired by a Zeiss NVision FIBSEM at a resolution of 10 nm per pixel.
source: A block face series of 32,000 images was acquired by a Zeiss NVision FIBSEM (Knott et al., 2008) at a resolution of 10 nm per pixel.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods, with citation to Knott et al., 2008.

claim: A focussed ion-beam was used to remove 2.5 nm of material from the sample block face.
source: A focussed ion-beam was used to remove 2.5 nm of material from the sample block face.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Consecutive sets of four images were summed to generate isotropic 10 nm voxels.
source: The images were aligned using affine transforms and consecutive sets of four images were summed to generate isotropic 10 nm voxels.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Manual annotation of pre- and postsynaptic sites took a total of ~6000 person-hours.
source: Manual annotation took a total of ~6000 person-hours to identify both pre- and postsynaptic sites, with 8–10 proofreaders working in parallel on different non-overlapping subsets of cubes.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental effort.

claim: Manual proofreading of the segmentation took a total of ~4000 person-hours.
source: This manual proofreading took a total of ~4000 person-hours, with 8–10 proofreaders working simultaneously on different non-overlapping subsets of cubes.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental effort.

claim: Putative excitatory inputs cluster at T4's dendrite shafts.
source: We uncover complex T4 inputs and reveal that putative excitatory inputs cluster at T4's dendrite shafts, while inhibitory inputs localize to the bases.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the connectome reconstruction.

claim: Inhibitory inputs localize to the bases of T4 dendrites.
source: We uncover complex T4 inputs and reveal that putative excitatory inputs cluster at T4's dendrite shafts, while inhibitory inputs localize to the bases.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the connectome reconstruction.

claim: Mi1 and Tm3 cells provide most synaptic contacts onto T4.
source: Consistent with our previous study, we reveal that Mi1 and Tm3 cells provide most synaptic contacts onto T4.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the connectome reconstruction.

claim: The study was unable to reproduce the spatial offset between Mi1 and Tm3 cells reported previously.
source: We are, however, unable to reproduce the spatial offset between these cells reported previously.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study.

claim: The comprehensive connectome reveals complex circuits that include candidate anatomical substrates for both HR and BL types of motion detectors.
source: Our comprehensive connectome reveals complex circuits that include candidate anatomical substrates for both HR and BL types of motion detectors.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's main conclusion.
